title: Expert gating warmup and cache interaction notes
content:
Summary:
This note collects experiments and hypotheses about transient latency and throughput degradation we observed when serving MoE-style models (mixture-of-experts) alongside dense models. The focus is on the interaction between gating behavior (expert selection hysteresis, switch frequency), KV-cache warmup/eviction, and short-term tail latency spikes during traffic shifts or bursty workloads.

Why this matters:
- Tail latency spikes of 50–300ms (beyond normal SLOs) seen in production while overall p99 throughput remains stable.
- These spikes correlate with bursts that cause repeated expert switches on hot prefixes, causing cache misses and non-amortized expert schedule churn.
- Mitigations that only target batching or autoscaling do not fully eliminate the problem because the root cause is routing + cache state.

Experiment setup (microbenchmarks):
- Models: MoE variant (70B-ish MoE config, 32 experts, 8 active per token) and dense baselines (70B dense and Mistral-variant 22B).
- Hardware: A100-80GB hosts with 1 model replica pinned; separate runs on H100 hosts for comparison.
- Sequence lengths: 32 (short), 512 (medium), 2048 (long).
- Batches: 1, 4, 16 typical; throughput-limited runs with concurrent user-shaped arrival processes.
- Instrumentation: per-request timers, per-expert invocation counters, per-expert KV hit/miss counters, gating softmax entropy, number of expert-switch events within prefix windows, and kernel-level stalls.

Observations (high-level):
1) Warmup window where gating is unstable:
   - Immediately after a cold start or after a long gap (>5s) of no traffic, the gating function shows higher entropy and higher variance in chosen expert sets for the same prefix. This lasts for O(10–100) requests per prefix.
   - During this window, we see repeated assignment to different expert subsets for adjacent tokens of the same request, creating more expert-switching overhead and extra KV-cache misses.

2) KV cache priming cost and asymmetric penalties:
   - When gating changes the chosen expert set, the receiving device often lacks the cached key/value shards for that expert for the current prefix, forcing it to rebuild KV state from scratch (costly for long prefix lengths).
   - We measured an extra 30–120ms per-token penalty on H100 when switching to previously-unused experts mid-request for seq_len >= 512.

3) Hotspot amplification from bursty traffic:
   - Short bursts (10–50qps) targeting a small set of prefixes cause repeated repeated hot-expert churn — the system alternates between a small set of experts per prefix but not consistently sticky, so the cache never reaches steady state.
   - Result: tail latency increases nonlinearly as batch sizes increase because the batching logic groups requests across different temporary expert sets, causing serialization and pipeline stalls.

4) Hardware variance:
   - A100 runs showed larger relative penalty on expert switches compared to H100 (likely due to different kernel launch and memory scheduling characteristics). Absolute times differ, but the qualitative pattern holds.

Diagnostic traces and key signals to surface in console:
- gating_entropy_per_token (distribution over time)
- expert_switch_count_per_request (and per-prefix rolling window)
- per_expert_kv_hit_rate (per minute)
- kernel_block_time (time waiting on memcpy/launch)
- request_prefix_id (to correlate repeated prefixes)
- p99_tail_by_prefix (to identify worst prefixes)

Hypotheses (root causes):
- Soft gating policies produce high variance early in a prefix's lifetime because the model's gating logits are sensitive to small context changes; model fine-tuning/temperature changes amplify this effect.
- The serving runtime treats experts as independent shards; switching to an unused shard forces synchronous KV population and kernel reconfiguration (no speculative prefetch).
- Batching that focuses on token count rather than expert locality mixes requests with incompatible expert sets, eliciting cross-expert contention.

Mitigations tried and results:
- Sticky gating (memoizing the chosen experts for the first N tokens of a prefix):
  Result: reduces expert switch_count_per_request by ~60% in microbenchmarks; tail latency improved by ~20–40% depending on batch size. Side-effect: slight decrease in model perplexity in a small fraction of samples (2–3%) — acceptable for production for many workloads.

- Prefetch window (speculatively populate KV shards for top-K likely experts for next M tokens):
  Result: reduced per-switch penalty from 30–120ms down to 10–30ms; increased memory usage by ~8% per replica. Need adaptive top-K selection to bound memory.

- Hysteresis on gating logits (add momentum/low-pass filter on logits before softmax):
  Result: smoothed gating_entropy; fewer micro-switches; minor CPU overhead. Clean wins in synthetic tests but requires model-level tuning to avoid harming quality.

- Batch grouping by expert-set affinity (best-effort):
  Result: improved pipeline utilization, but increases scheduling latency for some requests waiting to be grouped; net p99 improved in low-medium load, but not in high load.

- Per-expert rate limiting / backpressure:
  Result: protected hot experts from overload but caused fallback to alternate experts (tradeoffs). Needs careful SLAs per tenant.

Instrumentation/Runtime changes recommended (short-term):
1) Expose gating_entropy and expert_switch_count in the Console as first-class signals.
2) Add a lightweight sticky-routing shim which can be toggled per-route and has tunable token window (default 16 tokens).
3) Implement speculative prefetch for top-K experts chosen by a cheap predictor (cheap predictor could be recent history + gating logits).  Add a memory safety cap.
4) Introduce batcher-aware affinity heuristic: group by (route, prefix_hash, candidate_expert_fingerprint) with a bounded wait time (e.g., 3–6ms) to avoid unbounded scheduling delays.

Long-term/Model-level recommendations:
- Work with model onboarding team to evaluate gating regularization during fine-tuning (reduce softmax temperature, KL regularization across tokens) to increase gating stickiness without hurting accuracy.
- Consider a hybrid expert placement: co-locate frequently co-selected experts on the same device to reduce cross-device KV transfers.
- Explore composite KV layout that allows fast warm-up of a minimal KV subset when switching experts (compressed representation of recent keys).

Open questions / next experiments:
- How does sticky-routing interact with eval-based quality monitors (we saw tiny quality shifts but need systematic eval sets)?
- Can we build a cheap predictor for next-token expert set with >80% accuracy using only first N tokens of a request?
- Quantify memory vs latency tradeoff for prefetch top-K across fleet-wide distributions — simulate with realistic per-route traces.
- Measure behavior under mixed workloads (dense + MoE traffic) during autoscaler events.

Immediate action items (owner assignments):
- Maya: implement sticky-routing shim prototype in runtime (P0, 2w). Linked PR for prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/inference-runtime/pull/482
- Ravi: add gating_entropy and expert_switch_count to per-route metrics dashboard (P1, 1w).
- Hannah: assemble evaluation set and run quality regressions for sticky-routing at token windows [8,16,32] (P1, 2w).
- Carlos: run large-scale simulation with realistic prefix distributions and report memory/latency contours for prefetch top-K (P2, 3w).

Notes / rough log (chronological):
- 2024-09-12: first p99 spike reported during demo traffic; correlated with canary of MoE variant.
- 2024-09-20: microbenchmarks show expert switch penalty on H100 ~45ms for seq512; A100 shows ~90ms.
- 2024-09-27: sticky-routing prototype implemented locally, initial perf wins consistent.
- 2024-10-15: confirmed small quality drift on human eval samples; need broader eval.

If you poke at the traces: start by filtering requests with expert_switch_count_per_request > 4 and seq_len >= 256, then inspect gating_entropy evolution and kv_hit_rate for the implicated experts. That typically points to the prefix buckets causing the most pain.

Appendix: quick checklist for on-call when tail spike triggered:
- Check gating_entropy spike on the affected route.
- Check per-expert kv_hit_rate drops (cache thrash).
- If sticky-routing is enabled, check sticky-window exhaustion (are many requests bypassing sticky due to long gaps?).
- Consider short-term mitigation: enable route-level sticky-routing with window=8 and throttle prefetch memcap to 12% until root cause resolved.

End.
